overview.text: The sine function, written sin θ, assigns a number to an angle θ. For an acute angle in a right triangle, sine is the length of the opposite side divided by the hypotenuse. The function also applies to any real angle: if the angle’s terminal side meets the unit circle at (x, y), then sin θ is y, the point’s vertical coordinate. This connects triangle ratios with rotations and extends sine beyond right-triangle angles. As θ changes, sine repeats every 2π radians (360°) and stays between −1 and 1, producing its familiar wave-shaped graph. These properties make sine useful for finding unknown lengths and representing repeating patterns.

key_facts.text: In a right triangle, sin θ = opposite side ÷ hypotenuse.
On the unit circle, sin θ is the y-coordinate of the point corresponding to the angle.
The standard sine function has domain all real numbers and range [−1, 1].
Because sine tracks the unit-circle y-coordinate, its value is positive above the x-axis and negative below it.
